report.source_text: At day ten postextubation, she underwent an EEG. Frequent (2.5–4 Hz), florid bilateral, non-synchronous epileptiform discharges were seen over both hemispheres throughout most of the recording. The patient was unresponsive during this period of recording. 2mg of intravenous lorazepam was given, after which the epileptiform discharges subsided and a 6–7 Hz background predominated. The patient became slightly more alert, in that she could obey some motor commands and vocalise to a small extent.

report.source_text: One day later, she had another EEG study to investigate whether there were residual subclinical seizures. The EEG showed a background rhythm reaching 7–8 Hz, which was reactive to external stimulation. Frequent multifocal epileptiform discharges were seen as well as intermittent frontotemporal theta/delta waves. There was a significant improvement compared with the first EEG study. There was no evidence to suggest NCSE; however, frequent epileptiform discharges were seen over both hemispheres, without a clear focus (figure 1B).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 57-year-old woman with COPD, schizoaffective disorder, and recent pulmonary embolism presented in mid-April 2020 with acute respiratory failure (GCS 7, type 1 respiratory failure with PaO2 7.2 kPa, PaCO2 4.0 kPa, 91% saturation on 40% oxygen, hypotension, tachypnea RR 22) and fever. SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by RT-PCR. She was intubated the day after admission and mechanically ventilated for approximately one month. Following extubation, she remained altered and quadriplegic. Two days post-extubation, she developed new onset right-sided facial jerks and acute deterioration in mental status (less engaged, unable to speak or obey commands, opening eyes only to pain). EEG on day 10 post-extubation revealed frequent bilateral non-synchronous epileptiform discharges at 2.5-4 Hz consistent with NCSE. Lorazepam 2mg IV resulted in cessation of epileptiform activity and clinical improvement (increased alertness, ability to obey commands, vocalization). She was loaded on levetiracetam and continued on 500 mg twice daily. Follow-up EEG on day 11 post-extubation showed improvement with resolution of NCSE pattern and background rhythm reaching 7-8 Hz, though multifocal epileptiform discharges persisted. The patient gradually improved with recovery of speech and ability to obey commands. Three weeks after discharge to the neurology ward, she had episodes of fluctuating confusion associated with a concurrent urinary tract infection. Brain imaging (CT and MRI) performed post-extubation showed only mild age-related bilateral globus pallidus calcification on CT; MRI was normal.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: The acute onset of right-sided facial jerks, EEG findings of frequent bilateral epileptiform discharges, and dramatic response to lorazepam with cessation of EEG abnormalities and clinical improvement are inconsistent with psychiatric disease alone. The non-verbal state and altered mental status on admission were likely multifactorial (respiratory failure, fever, infection) but the acute deterioration post-extubation with seizure activity was clearly epileptic in nature.
CT brain showed only mild age-related bilateral globus pallidus calcification; MRI brain was normal. No acute structural abnormalities were identified to explain the seizure activity.

While metabolic derangements may have contributed to seizure susceptibility in the context of COVID-19, the specific EEG findings of frequent bilateral non-synchronous epileptiform discharges and the dramatic response to antiepileptic medications (lorazepam and levetiracetam) confirm NCSE as the primary diagnosis.
